title: Mock Test 1 — AIBE Sample Paper 3
examMeta: Nash Law Mock Test 1 · Based on AIBE Sample Paper 3 (100 MCQs · 210 Min)

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: A pre-Constitution statute that was inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III became void to the extent of the inconsistency on the commencement of the Constitution. The constitutional provision that renders such inconsistent laws void is:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 12

options.label: B
options.text: Article 31

options.label: C
options.text: Article 13

options.label: D
options.text: Article 35

rectification.principle: Article 13(1) declares all pre-Constitution laws, insofar as they are inconsistent with Part III, void to the extent of the inconsistency, and Article 13(2) bars the State from making any such law in future (Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates sometimes confuse Article 12 (definition of State) or Article 35 (Parliament's power to legislate on Fundamental Rights) with the voiding clause.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor Article 13 in Part III as the touchstone of Fundamental Rights validity: pre-Constitution laws are governed by Art. 13(1) and post-Constitution laws by Art. 13(2).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court held that the total reservation in favour of backward classes under Article 16(4) should ordinarily not exceed:

rectification.principle: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), a nine-judge Bench upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4) but fixed the ordinary total reservation ceiling at 50% save in extraordinary situations.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: 27% is frequently confused with the total ceiling when candidates mix up the OBC quota percentage with the overall vertical reservation cap.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Indra Sawhney = 27% OBC quota + 50% overall ceiling + creamy layer exclusion.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The principle that an unconstitutional law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not dead but merely dormant, and revives in its application to non-citizens or upon removal of the inconsistency by amendment, is known as the doctrine of:

options.label: A
options.text: Eclipse

options.label: B
options.text: Severability

options.label: C
options.text: Waiver

options.label: D
options.text: Pith and substance

rectification.principle: Under the Doctrine of Eclipse (Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P., 1955), a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not void ab initio but remains overshadowed/dormant against citizens and revives when the constitutional shadow is removed.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Severability and Eclipse both flow from Article 13, leading to mix-ups between cutting out offending clauses versus temporary overshadowing.
rectification.howToRectify: Link 'dormant but revivable' to Doctrine of Eclipse under Art. 13(1), and 'cutting away offending parts' to Severability.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: A statute contains some provisions that violate Fundamental Rights and others that are valid; the offending portions can be removed while the rest remains operative and workable. The principle applied to save the valid part is the doctrine of:

options.label: A
options.text: Eclipse

options.label: B
options.text: Colourable legislation

options.label: C
options.text: Harmonious construction

options.label: D
options.text: Severability

rectification.principle: The Doctrine of Severability (R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India, 1957) flows from the phrase 'to the extent of such inconsistency' in Article 13, allowing invalid portions to be severed if the remainder is workable.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing severability with harmonious construction (which reconciles conflicting statutory provisions rather than deleting unconstitutional ones).
rectification.howToRectify: Connect the Article 13 phrase 'to the extent of such inconsistency' directly to severability.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: A citizen voluntarily agrees not to claim the protection of a Fundamental Right. The settled constitutional position, affirmed in Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959), is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Fundamental Rights can be waived if waiver is in writing

options.label: B
options.text: Only the rights under Article 19 can be waived

options.label: C
options.text: There can be no waiver of Fundamental Rights

options.label: D
options.text: Waiver is permitted with the consent of the State

rectification.principle: In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Rights are conferred in the larger public interest as a constitutional command to the State and cannot be waived by an individual.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates sometimes import US constitutional doctrine (where personal rights can be waived) into Indian Part III jurisprudence.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember the absolute Indian rule from Basheshar Nath: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived, even in writing or by conduct.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: "Untouchability" is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden; any disability arising out of it is made an offence punishable in accordance with law. This is provided by:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 15

options.label: B
options.text: Article 17

options.label: C
options.text: Article 23

options.label: D
options.text: Article 18

rectification.principle: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form, enforceable even against private individuals and operationalized through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Article 15 (non-discrimination) and Article 18 (abolition of titles) sit adjacent in Right to Equality and are occasionally confused.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the Right to Equality sequence: 14 Equality, 15 Non-discrimination, 16 Public employment, 17 Untouchability, 18 Titles.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Court further directed that the "creamy layer" among the backward classes must be:

options.label: A
options.text: Excluded from the benefit of reservation

options.label: B
options.text: Given reservation in promotions

options.label: C
options.text: Treated as a separate forward class

options.label: D
options.text: Identified solely on the basis of caste

rectification.principle: In Indra Sawhney (1992), the Supreme Court mandated exclusion of the socially advanced 'creamy layer' from OBC reservation benefits under Article 16(4) so benefits reach genuinely backward sections.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusion arises over whether creamy layer applies to promotions or whether it reclassifies them legally as a separate class.
rectification.howToRectify: Note that creamy layer simply means exclusion from reservation benefits under Art. 16(4).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The right of all citizens "to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business" is guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g), but it is subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 19(2)

options.label: B
options.text: Article 19(5)

options.label: C
options.text: Article 19(4)

options.label: D
options.text: Article 19(6)

rectification.principle: Article 19(6) authorises reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public on the freedom of trade, occupation, and profession under Article 19(1)(g).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Because Art. 19(1)(f) was repealed, candidates sometimes misalign sub-clauses (d)/(e) with (5) and (g) with (5) instead of (6).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Article 20(2) embodies the protection against double jeopardy. According to its language and the decision in Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay (1953), the bar applies where a person has been:

options.label: A
options.text: Investigated for the same offence twice

options.label: B
options.text: Charged but acquitted before any court

options.label: C
options.text: Prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once

options.label: D
options.text: Tried before a departmental authority

rectification.principle: Article 20(2) incorporates nemo debet bis vexari pro una et eadem causa only in the form of autrefois convict: a person must have been both prosecuted AND punished before a court or judicial tribunal for the same offence (Maqbool Hussain v. State of Bombay).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse constitutional Art. 20(2) (which requires prior conviction/punishment) with statutory Section 300 CrPC (which covers both autrefois acquit and autrefois convict).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember the exact text of Art. 20(2): 'prosecuted AND punished' — both elements before a judicial court are mandatory.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Article 20(3) provides that no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), the Supreme Court held that the protection does NOT extend to:

options.label: A
options.text: A confession made to a magistrate

options.label: B
options.text: Giving of specimen signatures, handwriting or thumb impressions

options.label: C
options.text: An oral statement made under custodial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: A statement disclosing personal knowledge of the crime

rectification.principle: In State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961), an 11-judge Bench held that 'to be a witness' means imparting personal knowledge; giving physical specimens like handwriting, signatures, or thumb impressions for comparison is not testimonial compulsion under Art. 20(3).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming all compelled acts during police investigation violate self-incrimination rather than distinguishing testimonial vs. physical evidence.
rectification.howToRectify: Rule of Kathi Kalu Oghad: Art. 20(3) bars testimonial compulsion, not physical exemplars (handwriting, thumbprints, DNA/blood).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The right of children to free and compulsory education, made a Fundamental Right by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, is contained in:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 21A

options.label: B
options.text: Article 45

options.label: C
options.text: Article 41

options.label: D
options.text: Article 29

rectification.principle: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, guarantees free and compulsory education as a Fundamental Right for all children aged 6 to 14 years.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Article 45 (substituted by the same amendment for early childhood care below age 6) and Article 41 are Directive Principles, not Fundamental Rights.
rectification.howToRectify: Distinguish Art. 21A (FR for ages 6–14), Art. 45 (DPSP for below age 6), and Art. 51A(k) (Fundamental Duty of parents).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Article 22(1) and (2) guarantee safeguards on arrest, such as the right to be informed of grounds of arrest and to be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours. These particular safeguards do NOT apply to a person who is:

options.label: A
options.text: Arrested for a non-bailable offence

options.label: B
options.text: A foreign national

options.label: C
options.text: Arrested without a warrant

options.label: D
options.text: Detained under a law of preventive detention

rectification.principle: Article 22(3) expressly carves out two exceptions to the arrest safeguards in Articles 22(1) and (2): enemy aliens and any person arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates sometimes think foreign nationals generally lack Art. 22(1)-(2) rights, whereas only 'enemy aliens' and preventive detenus are excluded.
rectification.howToRectify: Read Art. 22(3) carefully: clauses (1) & (2) apply to punitive arrest; clauses (4)-(7) govern preventive detention.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Under Article 22(4), a person may ordinarily be detained under a preventive-detention law for a maximum period without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board of:

options.label: A
options.text: Two months

options.label: B
options.text: Six months

options.label: C
options.text: Three months

options.label: D
options.text: One month

rectification.principle: Article 22(4) mandates that no preventive detention law shall authorise detention for a period longer than three months unless an Advisory Board reports sufficient cause before the expiry of three months.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up the unnotified 44th Amendment change (two months) with the operative text of Article 22(4) (three months).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Article 22(4) in force = three months without Advisory Board approval.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The right to property, after the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, ceased to be a Fundamental Right and was made a constitutional/legal right. It now finds place in:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 31

options.label: B
options.text: Article 300A

options.label: C
options.text: Article 19(1)(f)

options.label: D
options.text: Article 39(b)

rectification.principle: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 repealed Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and inserted Article 300A in Part XII, stating no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Selecting the repealed Article 31 or 19(1)(f) instead of its relocated constitutional home in Part XII.
rectification.howToRectify: Link 44th Amendment (1978) -> deletion of Art. 19(1)(f) & 31 -> insertion of Art. 300A.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court interpreted the phrase "procedure established by law" in Article 21 to mean a procedure which is:

options.label: A
options.text: Right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive

options.label: B
options.text: Any procedure duly enacted by the legislature

options.label: C
options.text: The same as "due process of law" borrowed verbatim from the U.S.

options.label: D
options.text: Confined to the procedure prescribed by the Passport Act alone

rectification.principle: Overruling the narrow A.K. Gopalan view, Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) held that 'procedure established by law' under Art. 21 must be right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive, linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 (Golden Triangle).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the substantive fairness standard adopted by the Court with literal adoption of the US textual phrase 'due process of law'.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember Maneka Gandhi's exact formula: procedure must be 'just, fair and reasonable', not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held, by majority, that Parliament:

options.label: A
options.text: Could amend Fundamental Rights only with ratification by the States

options.label: B
options.text: Possessed unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution

options.label: C
options.text: Could amend Fundamental Rights subject to the basic-structure doctrine

options.label: D
options.text: Had no power to amend Part III so as to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights

rectification.principle: In Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), an 11-judge Bench (6:5) treated a constitutional amendment as 'law' under Art. 13(2) and held Parliament had no power to amend Part III to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights (prospectively overruled in Kesavananda Bharati).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Conflating Golak Nath (1967, no power to abridge FRs) with Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure doctrine).
rectification.howToRectify: Track the trilogy: Shankari Prasad (unlimited) -> Golak Nath (Part III unamendable) -> Kesavananda Bharati (amendable except Basic Structure).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The President may promulgate an Ordinance when both Houses of Parliament are not in session and circumstances exist that render immediate action necessary. This power is conferred by:

options.label: A
options.text: Article 213

options.label: B
options.text: Article 356

options.label: C
options.text: Article 123

options.label: D
options.text: Article 352

rectification.principle: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate Ordinances during the recess of Parliament, having the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Swapping digits between Article 123 (President's Ordinance) and Article 213 (Governor's Ordinance).
rectification.howToRectify: Mnemonic: Union comes first (1-2-3 = President); State Governor comes second (2-1-3 = Governor).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and ceases to operate at the expiration of a period from the reassembly of Parliament unless approved earlier. That period is:

options.label: A
options.text: Four weeks

options.label: B
options.text: Six weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Two months

options.label: D
options.text: Three months

rectification.principle: Under Article 123(2)(a), an Ordinance must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament (counted from the later date if Houses reassemble on different dates).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the 6-month maximum gap between parliamentary sessions (Art. 85) with the 6-week post-reassembly window for Ordinance approval.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize: 6 months max recess + 6 weeks after reassembly = maximum Ordinance life of 6 months and 6 weeks.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The protection of Article 15(1) against discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth is available:

options.label: A
options.text: Only to citizens of India

options.label: B
options.text: To citizens and foreigners alike

options.label: C
options.text: Only to members of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes

options.label: D
options.text: Only against private individuals

rectification.principle: Article 15(1) opens with 'The State shall not discriminate against any citizen...', making it a citizens-only Fundamental Right (alongside Articles 16, 19, 29, and 30).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Extending Article 14's 'any person' phrasing (which covers foreigners too) to Article 15.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the five Fundamental Rights exclusive to citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A police officer, acting in good faith and under a belief based on a wrong understanding of the law that he was empowered to arrest X without a warrant, makes the arrest. He cannot claim protection under s.79 IPC because that section excuses only a:

options.label: A
options.text: Mistake of fact made in good faith

options.label: B
options.text: Mistake of law made in good faith

options.label: C
options.text: Mistake by a public servant only

options.label: D
options.text: Mistake induced by superior orders

rectification.principle: Sections 76 and 79 IPC embody 'ignorantia facti excusat, ignorantia juris non excusat': only a mistake of fact made in good faith excuses criminal liability, never a mistake of law.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming 'good faith' rescues an honest misunderstanding of statutory arrest powers.
rectification.howToRectify: Check whether the error concerns a fact or a legal rule: mistake of fact = excused (s.76/79); mistake of law = no defence.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A judge, acting judicially in the exercise of a power which he in good faith believes is given to him by law, passes an order that later turns out to be without jurisdiction. Which General Exception protects him from criminal liability?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 76 IPC

options.label: B
options.text: Section 77 IPC

options.label: C
options.text: Section 78 IPC

options.label: D
options.text: Section 79 IPC

rectification.principle: Section 77 IPC protects a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing Section 77 (act of Judge acting judicially) with Section 78 (act done by ministerial officer pursuant to judgment/order of Court).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair ss.77–78 IPC: 77 = Judge acting judicially; 78 = officer executing Court's order.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A is at work with a hatchet; the head flies off and kills a bystander. A had taken proper precautions and there was no criminal intention. The act is excused as an accident under s.80 IPC only if it was done:

options.label: A
options.text: In a lawful manner, by lawful means, with proper care and caution

options.label: B
options.text: In the exercise of private defence

options.label: C
options.text: Under grave and sudden provocation

options.label: D
options.text: Under a mistake of law in good faith

rectification.principle: Section 80 IPC (reproducing the statutory hatchet illustration) excuses an act done by accident or misfortune without criminal intention or knowledge in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means and with proper care and caution.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Overlooking that all three 'lawful' elements plus 'proper care and caution' are cumulative prerequisites under s.80.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the four elements of s.80 IPC: no mens rea + lawful act + lawful manner & means + proper care and caution.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A, the captain of a vessel, suddenly and without any fault on his part finds himself in a position where, to save the lives of many passengers, he must run down a small boat with two persons aboard. If he acts in good faith to avert the greater harm, he may claim the benefit of:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 81 IPC (necessity — act likely to cause harm done to prevent greater harm)

options.label: B
options.text: Section 80 IPC (accident)

options.label: C
options.text: Section 87 IPC (consent)

options.label: D
options.text: Section 82 IPC (act of a child)

rectification.principle: Illustration (a) to Section 81 IPC covers the captain choosing the lesser harm in good faith without criminal intent to prevent greater harm (doctrine of necessity / jus necessitatis).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing intentional choice of a lesser evil (s.81 necessity) with unintended mishap (s.80 accident).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.80 = unintended accident; s.81 = knowing act done in good faith to prevent greater imminent harm.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Under the IPC, nothing is an offence which is done by a child. Which statement correctly states the rule on infancy?

options.label: A
options.text: A child under twelve years can never be held liable

options.label: B
options.text: A child under ten years is absolutely exempt and there is no upper conditional age

options.label: C
options.text: A child under seven is exempt only if of immature understanding

options.label: D
options.text: A child under seven years (s.82) is absolutely exempt; a child of seven but under twelve (s.83) is exempt only if not of sufficient maturity of understanding

rectification.principle: Section 82 grants absolute immunity to a child under 7 years (doli incapax), while Section 83 grants qualified immunity to a child between 7 and 12 years who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up the absolute boundary (under 7) with the qualified boundary (7 to under 12).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize: s.82 = under 7 (absolute); s.83 = 7 to under 12 (conditional on immaturity).

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: The presumption that a child below the age of seven cannot commit a crime because it lacks the capacity to form criminal intent is expressed by which Latin maxim, reflected in s.82 IPC?

options.label: A
options.text: Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea

options.label: B
options.text: Doli incapax

options.label: C
options.text: Volenti non fit injuria

options.label: D
options.text: Ignorantia facti excusat

rectification.principle: Doli incapax ('incapable of crime/evil') is the irrebuttable legal presumption under s.82 IPC that a child under 7 years cannot form criminal intent.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Selecting the general mens rea maxim (actus non facit reum...) instead of the specific infancy maxim.
rectification.howToRectify: Associate 'doli incapax' directly with s.82 IPC (child under 7).

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: The test of legal insanity under s.84 IPC is derived from the McNaughten (M'Naghten) Rules. To claim the exception, the accused must show that, by reason of unsoundness of mind, at the time of the act he was incapable of:

options.label: A
options.text: Controlling any of his emotions or impulses

options.label: B
options.text: Remembering the act after it was committed

options.label: C
options.text: Knowing the nature of the act, or that it was either wrong or contrary to law

options.label: D
options.text: Understanding the consequences of imprisonment

rectification.principle: Section 84 IPC codifies the cognitive McNaughten test: at the time of doing the act, by reason of unsoundness of mind, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he was doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing cognitive incapacity (knowing nature/wrongfulness) with irresistible impulse (volitional lack of self-control, which s.84 does not accept).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the two prongs of s.84: didn't know nature of act, OR didn't know it was wrong/contrary to law.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes "medical insanity" from "legal insanity" for the purposes of s.84 IPC?

options.label: A
options.text: They are identical; any mental illness is a defence

options.label: B
options.text: Medical insanity is a complete defence but legal insanity is only a mitigating factor

options.label: C
options.text: Only medical insanity certified before the act is relevant

options.label: D
options.text: Legal insanity, not mere medical insanity, must be proved — the accused must lack the cognitive capacity described in s.84 at the time of the act

rectification.principle: Courts consistently hold (Surendra Mishra v. State of Jharkhand; Hari Singh Gond v. State of M.P.) that mere medical diagnosis of mental disorder is insufficient; legal insanity—loss of cognitive capacity under s.84 at the exact time of the act—must be proved.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming any psychiatric diagnosis automatically triggers an acquittal under s.84.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.84 requires 'legal insanity' (impairment of cognitive faculties at the moment of the offence), not mere medical illness.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: X voluntarily becomes drunk and, in that state, kills Y. As to the effect of voluntary intoxication on criminal liability under ss.85–86 IPC, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Voluntary intoxication is a complete defence like involuntary intoxication

options.label: B
options.text: Voluntary intoxication is no defence; the accused is treated as having the same knowledge he would have had if not intoxicated, though specific intent may still be assessed

options.label: C
options.text: Voluntary intoxication automatically reduces every offence to a lesser one

options.label: D
options.text: Voluntary intoxication is relevant only to sentencing, never to knowledge or intent

rectification.principle: Under s.85 IPC only involuntary intoxication is a defence; under s.86 IPC (Basdev v. State of Pepsu), a voluntarily intoxicated person is presumed to have the same knowledge as a sober person, while specific intention is judged from facts and circumstances.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Overlooking the distinction in s.86 between imputed 'knowledge' and un-imputed 'specific intent'.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember Basdev v. State of Pepsu: s.85 = involuntary; s.86 = voluntary drunkenness gives no excuse and imputes sober knowledge.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A, above eighteen years of age, consents to fence with B for amusement and is hurt without foul play. B is protected because, under s.87 IPC, the consent operates where the act is not intended and not known to be likely to cause:

options.label: A
options.text: Any hurt whatsoever

options.label: B
options.text: Simple hurt only

options.label: C
options.text: Death or grievous hurt

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of property

rectification.principle: Section 87 IPC protects acts done with consent of a person above 18 (e.g., fencing/sports without foul play) provided the act is neither intended nor known to be likely to cause death or grievous hurt.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.87 (barring death/grievous hurt) with s.88 (good faith acts for benefit where even risk of death is protected).
rectification.howToRectify: Contrast s.87 (sport/amusement: not intended/known likely to cause death or grievous hurt) vs s.88 (medical/benefit: even if death is likely, provided not intended).

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A surgeon, in good faith and for the patient's benefit, performs a risky operation to which the patient (an adult) has consented, knowing it may cause death. Even if the patient dies, the surgeon is protected. Which section embodies this rule on consent to acts done in good faith for a person's benefit?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 87 IPC

options.label: B
options.text: Section 88 IPC

options.label: C
options.text: Section 92 IPC

options.label: D
options.text: Section 95 IPC

rectification.principle: Section 88 IPC protects acts not intended to cause death, done in good faith for the benefit of a person who consented (expressly or impliedly), even when known to be likely to cause death (e.g., risky surgery).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up s.88 (consenting adult patient) with s.92 (unconscious/emergency patient without consent).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember the surgical trilogy: s.88 = adult consents; s.89 = guardian consents for child/unsound person; s.92 = emergency without consent.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A consent given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact, or by a person of unsound mind or by a child under twelve, is not a valid consent for the purposes of the consent-based exceptions. This limitation on what counts as "consent" is laid down in:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 90 IPC

options.label: B
options.text: Section 91 IPC

options.label: C
options.text: Section 93 IPC

options.label: D
options.text: Section 94 IPC

rectification.principle: Section 90 IPC defines vitiated/invalid consent: consent given under fear of injury, misconception of fact (known to the doer), unsoundness of mind/intoxication, or by a child under 12 years.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.90 (what is NOT consent) with s.91 (acts that are offences independently of harm caused).
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor s.90 IPC as the negative definition of consent across the entire Penal Code.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: A, in a crowded train, slightly jostles B without intending harm and causing only the trivial annoyance ordinarily incidental to travel. No offence is made out because of the maxim de minimis non curat lex, codified in:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 93 IPC

options.label: B
options.text: Section 94 IPC

options.label: C
options.text: Section 95 IPC

options.label: D
options.text: Section 96 IPC

rectification.principle: Section 95 IPC codifies de minimis non curat lex ('the law takes no account of trifles'), excusing acts causing harm so slight that no person of ordinary sense and temper would complain of it.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.94 (compulsion by threat of instant death) or s.96 (private defence) with s.95 (trivial harm).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.95 = last section before Private Defence (ss.96–106) = de minimis non curat lex.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Under s.107 IPC, a person abets the doing of a thing in three distinct ways. Which of the following is NOT one of the three modes of abetment?

options.label: A
options.text: Instigating any person to do that thing

options.label: B
options.text: Engaging in a conspiracy for the doing of that thing

options.label: C
options.text: Intentionally aiding, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing

options.label: D
options.text: Merely entertaining a wish that the thing be done

rectification.principle: Section 107 IPC specifies exactly three modes of abetment: (1) Instigation, (2) Conspiracy (with an act/illegal omission in pursuance), and (3) Intentional aiding. Mere passive wishing is no crime.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Rushing through the 'NOT' prompt and selecting one of the three valid statutory limbs.
rectification.howToRectify: Check negative phrasing carefully and recall s.107's triad: Instigate, Conspire (+ act), Intentionally Aid.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes abetment by conspiracy (s.107 Secondly) from the substantive offence of criminal conspiracy (s.120A IPC)?

options.label: A
options.text: Abetment by conspiracy requires an act or illegal omission in pursuance of the conspiracy and that the thing be done, whereas criminal conspiracy under s.120A is complete on the agreement itself (an overt act being required only where the object is not an offence)

options.label: B
options.text: They are identical and always charged together

options.label: C
options.text: For abetment by conspiracy a mere agreement suffices and nothing more is ever needed

options.label: D
options.text: Criminal conspiracy can only be committed by public servants

rectification.principle: Under s.107 Secondly, abetment by conspiracy requires an act or illegal omission taking place in pursuance of the conspiracy, whereas s.120A makes the bare agreement to commit an offence punishable as a substantive crime (overt act needed only if the agreed act is illegal though not an offence).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming mere agreement constitutes abetment by conspiracy under s.107 without any overt act.
rectification.howToRectify: Contrast: s.120A = agreement alone (for offences); s.107 Secondly = agreement + act or illegal omission in pursuance.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Where the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made for its punishment, the abettor is punished under s.109 IPC with:

options.label: A
options.text: Half the punishment provided for the offence abetted

options.label: B
options.text: The punishment provided for the offence abetted

options.label: C
options.text: Only a fine in every case

options.label: D
options.text: Imprisonment not exceeding six months in all cases

rectification.principle: Under Section 109 IPC, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment and no express punishment is prescribed elsewhere, the abettor receives the same punishment provided for the offence itself.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.109 (act committed -> full punishment) with ss.115/116 (offence NOT committed -> fraction of punishment).
rectification.howToRectify: Separate abetment punishment rules: s.109 (committed = full punishment) vs ss.115–116 (not committed = reduced punishment).

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: Section 34 IPC requires a "common intention". In Mahbub Shah v. Emperor, the Privy Council clarified that common intention must be distinguished from:

options.label: A
options.text: A premeditated concert

options.label: B
options.text: A prearranged plan

options.label: C
options.text: A similar intention independently entertained by different persons

options.label: D
options.text: A meeting of minds before the act

rectification.principle: In Mahbub Shah v. Emperor (1945), the Privy Council emphasized the dividing line between 'common intention' (prearranged plan/meeting of minds) and 'same or similar intention' independently formed without prior concert.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Misreading 'distinguished from' and picking features that describe common intention itself.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember Mahbub Shah's core warning: common intention != same/similar intention.

questions.subject: Indian Penal Code / BNS
questions.question: According to Mahbub Shah v. Emperor, the existence of common intention under s.34 IPC:

options.label: A
options.text: Must always be proved by direct evidence of a prior agreement in writing

options.label: B
options.text: Can never be inferred and must be admitted by the accused

options.label: C
options.text: Is presumed whenever two or more persons are present at the scene

options.label: D
options.text: May be inferred from the conduct of the accused and the circumstances, but the prearranged plan may develop on the spot

rectification.principle: Common intention is rarely capable of direct proof and must be inferred from conduct and surrounding circumstances; while it implies a prearranged plan, that concert may develop even on the spur of the moment at the scene (Mahbub Shah; Pandurang).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking 'prearranged plan' requires days of planning rather than an on-the-spot meeting of minds.
rectification.howToRectify: Note: Common intention = inferred from conduct + circumstances, and concert can develop on the spot.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Under the scheme of criminal courts in s.6 read with ss.26–29 CrPC, which court is the highest trial court in a district empowered to pass any sentence authorised by law (subject to confirmation of a death sentence by the High Court)?

options.label: A
options.text: Court of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class

options.label: B
options.text: Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate

options.label: C
options.text: Court of Session

options.label: D
options.text: Court of a Metropolitan Magistrate

rectification.principle: Under Section 28(2) CrPC, a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge may pass any sentence authorised by law, but any sentence of death passed by such Judge is subject to confirmation by the High Court under s.366 CrPC.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the Chief Judicial Magistrate (highest Magisterial court, capped at 7 years) with the Court of Session (highest district trial court).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize hierarchy under ss.28–29 CrPC: JMFC/MM (3 yrs) < Assistant Sessions Judge (10 yrs) < CJM (7 yrs) < Sessions Judge (any sentence; death needs HC confirmation).

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Under s.29 CrPC, a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding:

options.label: A
options.text: One year

options.label: B
options.text: Two years

options.label: C
options.text: Three years

options.label: D
options.text: Seven years

rectification.principle: Section 29(2) CrPC empowers a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class (and Metropolitan Magistrate under s.29(4)) to pass imprisonment not exceeding three years.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up JMFC (3 years) with JMFC Second Class (1 year under s.29(3)) or CJM (7 years under s.29(1)).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize s.29 CrPC limits: CJM = 7 years; JMFC/MM = 3 years; JMSC = 1 year.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Under s.29 CrPC, a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding:

options.label: A
options.text: Three years

options.label: B
options.text: Five years

options.label: C
options.text: Ten years

options.label: D
options.text: Seven years

rectification.principle: Section 29(1) CrPC caps the sentencing power of a Chief Judicial Magistrate (and Chief Metropolitan Magistrate) at imprisonment not exceeding seven years (excluding death or life imprisonment).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing CJM (7 years) with Assistant Sessions Judge (10 years under s.28(3)).
rectification.howToRectify: Keep s.28(3) (ASJ = 10 yrs) distinct from s.29(1) (CJM = 7 yrs).

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: The act by which a Magistrate first takes judicial notice of an offence with a view to initiating proceedings is called "taking cognizance." The modes of taking cognizance by a Magistrate are set out in:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 190 CrPC

options.label: B
options.text: Section 154 CrPC

options.label: C
options.text: Section 173 CrPC

options.label: D
options.text: Section 200 CrPC

rectification.principle: Section 190(1) CrPC enumerates the three sources on which a Magistrate may take cognizance: (a) complaint, (b) police report, or (c) information from any person other than a police officer or own knowledge.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.190 (taking cognizance) with s.200 (examination of complainant after cognizance on a complaint).
rectification.howToRectify: Trace Chapter XIV CrPC: s.190 opens 'Conditions Requisite for Initiation of Proceedings' -> taking cognizance.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a "complaint" from an "FIR" under the CrPC?

options.label: A
options.text: A complaint must always relate to a cognizable offence and is made to the police

options.label: B
options.text: An FIR can be filed only before a Magistrate and a complaint only before the police

options.label: C
options.text: A complaint is an allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate (with a view to his taking action) and, by definition in s.2(d), does not include a police report; an FIR under s.154 is information about a cognizable offence given to the police

options.label: D
options.text: There is no legal difference between the two

rectification.principle: Section 2(d) CrPC defines a complaint as an allegation to a Magistrate (excluding a police report, covering cognizable or non-cognizable offences), while s.154 FIR is first information of a cognizable offence given to a police officer.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Colloquial use of 'police complaint' obscures the strict CrPC s.2(d) definition.
rectification.howToRectify: Always pair s.2(d) Complaint -> to Magistrate (excludes police report); s.154 FIR -> to Police (cognizable offence only).

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Under s.2(w) and s.2(x) CrPC, the distinction between a "summons-case" and a "warrant-case" turns on:

options.label: A
options.text: Whether the accused is in custody

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the case is instituted on a complaint or a police report

options.label: C
options.text: Whether the offence is bailable

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the offence is punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment exceeding two years (warrant-case) or not (summons-case)

rectification.principle: Section 2(x) defines a warrant-case as an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment exceeding two years; s.2(w) defines a summons-case as any case relating to an offence not being a warrant-case.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing summons/warrant classification (punishment threshold > 2 years) with bailable/non-bailable or cognizable/non-cognizable.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the threshold: > 2 years / life / death = Warrant-case (s.2(x)); <= 2 years = Summons-case (s.2(w)).

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure Code / BNSS
questions.question: Regarding the compounding of offences under s.320 CrPC, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Every offence under the IPC can be compounded by the parties

options.label: B
options.text: Some offences may be compounded by the specified persons without the court, while certain others may be compounded only with the permission of the court; offences not listed are non-compoundable

options.label: C
options.text: All offences may be compounded only with the permission of the Supreme Court

options.label: D
options.text: Compounding of an offence always results in conviction with a reduced sentence

rectification.principle: Section 320 CrPC contains two tables: s.320(1) lists offences compoundable by the victim without court permission, s.320(2) lists offences compoundable only with court permission, and s.320(9) bars compounding of any other offence. Valid compounding has the effect of acquittal (s.320(8)).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking compounding requires High Court/SC quashing (s.482) or results in a reduced sentence instead of acquittal.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.320 CrPC: Table 1 (no court leave) + Table 2 (with court leave) + s.320(8) (acquittal).

questions.subject: Indian Evidence Act / BSA
questions.question: A villager runs from his hut to the police station and, panting, shouts that "Z has just stabbed B," the statement being made immediately upon and during the transaction. Such a spontaneous statement forming part of the same transaction is relevant as part of the res gestae under:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872

options.label: B
options.text: Section 5 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872

options.label: C
options.text: Section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872

options.label: D
options.text: Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872

rectification.principle: Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 embodies the doctrine of res gestae: facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction (spontaneous, contemporaneous utterances) are relevant.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing spontaneous res gestae (s.6) with subsequent conduct or explanatory statements (s.8).
rectification.howToRectify: Look for spontaneity and immediacy ('during or immediately after the transaction') -> Section 6 res gestae.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a suit for compensation for wrong done to the person where the wrong was done within the local limits of one court but the defendant resides within the limits of another court may be instituted, under Section 19, in:

options.label: A
options.text: the court within whose limits the wrong was done or where the defendant resides or carries on business, at the plaintiff's option

options.label: B
options.text: only the court within whose limits the defendant resides

options.label: C
options.text: only the court within whose limits the wrong was done

options.label: D
options.text: the court of the highest pecuniary jurisdiction in the State

rectification.principle: Section 19 CPC governs suits for compensation for wrongs to person or movables, granting the plaintiff the option to sue either where the wrong was done or where the defendant resides, carries on business, or personally works for gain.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Restricting jurisdiction solely to the place of wrong or solely to the defendant's residence.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize s.19 CPC: wrong to person/movables = place of wrong OR defendant's residence/business (plaintiff's choice).

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Under Section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a suit not otherwise provided for may be instituted in a court within whose local limits:

options.label: A
options.text: only the cause of action wholly arises

options.label: B
options.text: the defendant actually and voluntarily resides or carries on business, or the cause of action wholly or in part arises

options.label: C
options.text: only the plaintiff resides

options.label: D
options.text: the immovable property in dispute is situated, irrespective of the cause of action

rectification.principle: Section 20 CPC is the residuary place-of-suing rule: a suit may be filed where the defendant resides/carries on business/works for gain, or where the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mistakenly believing the cause of action must arise 'wholly' or that the plaintiff's residence confers general territorial jurisdiction.
rectification.howToRectify: Note two key rules in s.20 CPC: defendant's place (never plaintiff's!) OR cause of action 'wholly OR in part'.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: An objection to the place of suing (territorial jurisdiction) under Section 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 will be allowed by an appellate or revisional court only if it was:

options.label: A
options.text: taken in the court of first instance at the earliest possible opportunity, and there has been a consequent failure of justice

options.label: B
options.text: raised for the first time in the appellate court

options.label: C
options.text: supported by a separate written application at any stage

options.label: D
options.text: never waived, since territorial jurisdiction can never be conferred by consent

rectification.principle: Under Section 21 CPC (Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan), an appellate/revisional court will entertain an objection to territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction only if (1) taken in the trial court at the earliest opportunity (at or before settlement of issues) AND (2) there has been a consequent failure of justice.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing subject-matter jurisdiction (inherent lack of jurisdiction, which cannot be waived) with territorial/pecuniary jurisdiction (which can be waived under s.21).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.21 CPC's twin test: earliest opportunity + consequent failure of justice.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, an amendment of pleadings after the trial has commenced shall not be allowed unless the court is satisfied that:

options.label: A
options.text: the opposite party consents in writing

options.label: B
options.text: the amendment adds a wholly new cause of action

options.label: C
options.text: in spite of due diligence the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of trial

options.label: D
options.text: the amendment is sought before the framing of issues

rectification.principle: The 2002 proviso to Order VI Rule 17 CPC (upheld in Salem Advocate Bar Association v. Union of India) bars post-trial amendments unless the court concludes that in spite of due diligence the party could not raise the matter before trial commenced.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying the pre-2002 liberal standard ('at any stage') without applying the mandatory post-trial due-diligence proviso.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor Order VI Rule 17 Proviso: once trial begins, 'due diligence' is the strict gatekeeper.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: A defendant who has against the plaintiff an ascertained sum of money legally recoverable may, in a suit for recovery of money, plead it by way of:

options.label: A
options.text: a fresh independent plaint only

options.label: B
options.text: a written statement of admission

options.label: C
options.text: an application for review under Order XLVII

options.label: D
options.text: a set-off under Order VIII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

rectification.principle: Under Order VIII Rule 6 CPC, in a suit for recovery of money, the defendant may claim a legal set-off in his written statement of any ascertained sum of money legally recoverable by him from the plaintiff within the court's pecuniary jurisdiction.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking cross-claims always require a separate fresh suit.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Order VIII Rule 6 = legal set-off (ascertained money claim pleaded in written statement).

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: The essential distinction between a legal set-off (Order VIII Rule 6) and a counterclaim (Order VIII Rule 6A) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is that:

options.label: A
options.text: a set-off may exceed the plaintiff's claim, but a counterclaim cannot

options.label: B
options.text: a counterclaim is confined to an ascertained sum of money, while a set-off may be of any nature

options.label: C
options.text: a set-off must be for an ascertained sum within the court's pecuniary jurisdiction, whereas a counterclaim is treated as a cross-suit and may exceed the plaintiff's claim

options.label: D
options.text: both must arise out of the same transaction as the plaintiff's claim

rectification.principle: A legal set-off (Order VIII Rule 6) is a statutory defence confined to an ascertained sum of money within pecuniary limits, whereas a counterclaim (Order VIII Rule 6A) acts as an independent cross-suit for any right/claim and can exceed the plaintiff's claim.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Reversing the attributes of set-off (defence, ascertained money) and counterclaim (cross-suit, any claim).
rectification.howToRectify: Rule of thumb: Set-off = shield (ascertained money); Counterclaim = sword + cross-suit (can exceed plaintiff's claim).

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Under Order I Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a suit shall not be defeated by reason of misjoinder or non-joinder of parties; however, this saving does NOT apply where there is non-joinder of a:

options.label: A
options.text: proper party

options.label: B
options.text: necessary party

options.label: C
options.text: pro forma defendant

options.label: D
options.text: party added merely for convenience

rectification.principle: The proviso to Order I Rule 9 CPC clarifies that nothing in Rule 9 applies to non-joinder of a necessary party—without whom no effective decree can be passed—rendering such non-joinder fatal to the suit.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing 'proper party' (whose presence helps completely adjudicate) with 'necessary party' (without whom no effective order can be made).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize: non-joinder of proper party != fatal; non-joinder of necessary party = fatal (O1 R9 proviso).

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Under Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, issues arise when:

options.label: A
options.text: the plaint is presented

options.label: B
options.text: the parties file a joint memorandum

options.label: C
options.text: a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by one party and denied by the other

options.label: D
options.text: the court delivers judgment

rectification.principle: Order XIV Rule 1(1) CPC states that issues arise when a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by one party and denied by the other.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the stage of filing pleadings with the legal definition of how an issue arises.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember the exact statutory trigger in Order XIV Rule 1: 'affirmed by one party and denied by the other'.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.question: Where a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may, under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, apply to set it aside on the ground that:

options.label: A
options.text: the decree is erroneous on the merits

options.label: B
options.text: the summons was not duly served, or he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing

options.label: C
options.text: the plaintiff has not executed the decree within one year

options.label: D
options.text: a fresh suit on the same cause of action is pending

rectification.principle: Order IX Rule 13 CPC limits setting aside an ex parte decree to two grounds: (1) summons was not duly served, or (2) the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming merits errors can be argued under Order IX Rule 13 (merits challenges require an appeal under s.96(2) or review).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize Order IX Rule 13's two exclusive grounds: no due service OR sufficient cause for non-appearance.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), the Privy Council held that an agreement entered into by a minor is:

options.label: A
options.text: void ab initio

options.label: B
options.text: voidable at the option of the minor

options.label: C
options.text: valid if ratified by the minor on attaining majority

options.label: D
options.text: enforceable to the extent of benefit received

rectification.principle: In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), interpreting Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the Privy Council held that a minor is incompetent to contract and a minor's agreement is absolutely void ab initio (void from the very beginning), not voidable or ratifiable.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing Indian law (void ab initio) with English common law (where some minor contracts are voidable).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Mohori Bibee = minor's agreement is void ab initio under s.11 Contract Act.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: Under Section 15 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, "coercion" is the committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code, or:

options.label: A
options.text: the dominating of the will of another by a party in a fiduciary relationship

options.label: B
options.text: a false statement of fact honestly believed to be true

options.label: C
options.text: the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge of it

options.label: D
options.text: the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing him to enter into an agreement

rectification.principle: Section 15 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines coercion in two limbs: committing/threatening an act forbidden by the IPC, OR the unlawful detaining/threatening to detain any property to the prejudice of any person to induce an agreement.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing coercion (s.15) with undue influence (s.16, dominating will), fraud (s.17, active concealment), or misrepresentation (s.18).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize s.15's two limbs: IPC-forbidden act OR unlawful detention of property.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: Under Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract is said to be induced by "undue influence" where:

options.label: A
options.text: one party makes a false statement intending the other to act on it

options.label: B
options.text: consent is obtained by a threat to detain property

options.label: C
options.text: the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage

options.label: D
options.text: a fact material to the contract is innocently misstated

rectification.principle: Section 16(1) of the Indian Contract Act requires two cumulative ingredients for undue influence: (1) one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other, and (2) uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing moral/psychological pressure from a dominant relationship (s.16) with physical/property threats (s.15 coercion).
rectification.howToRectify: Map ss.15–18 Contract Act: 15 Coercion, 16 Undue influence (dominate will + unfair advantage), 17 Fraud, 18 Misrepresentation.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: The essential difference between fraud (Section 17) and misrepresentation (Section 18) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is that:

options.label: A
options.text: fraud renders the contract void, while misrepresentation renders it valid

options.label: B
options.text: fraud involves an intention to deceive, whereas misrepresentation is an innocent or unintentional false assertion believed to be true

options.label: C
options.text: misrepresentation requires active concealment, while fraud does not

options.label: D
options.text: only misrepresentation gives the aggrieved party a right to rescind

rectification.principle: Both fraud (s.17) and misrepresentation (s.18) make a contract voidable under s.19, but fraud requires an intention to deceive (no honest belief or active concealment), whereas misrepresentation is an innocent false assertion believed to be true.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming fraud makes the contract void (it is voidable under s.19, plus damages are available).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.17 Fraud = intent to deceive (voidable + damages); s.18 Misrepresentation = innocent misstatement (voidable).

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Under the principle of vicarious liability in the law of torts, a master is liable for the tort of his servant only where the wrongful act is committed:

options.label: A
options.text: in the course of the servant's employment

options.label: B
options.text: at any time while the servant is employed by him

options.label: C
options.text: only when the master has expressly authorised the wrongful act

options.label: D
options.text: only if the servant is acting for the master's personal benefit

rectification.principle: Under respondeat superior / qui facit per alium facit per se (State Bank of India v. Shyama Devi), a master is vicariously liable for a servant's torts committed 'in the course of employment'—including unauthorized modes of doing authorized work.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking express authorization is required or that every act during employment hours binds the employer.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor the Salmond test: master is liable if the tort falls 'in the course of employment'.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Where the damage to the plaintiff is caused partly by his own negligence and partly by the negligence of the defendant, the resulting defence or apportionment in the law of torts is known as:

options.label: A
options.text: composite negligence

options.label: B
options.text: absolute liability

options.label: C
options.text: nervous shock

options.label: D
options.text: contributory negligence

rectification.principle: Contributory negligence arises when the plaintiff's own lack of care combines with the defendant's negligence to cause the harm, leading to apportionment of damages (Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Laxman Iyer).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing contributory negligence (plaintiff + defendant both negligent) with composite negligence (two or more independent defendants negligent, plaintiff innocent).
rectification.howToRectify: Rule: plaintiff also at fault = contributory negligence; multiple defendants at fault = composite negligence.

questions.subject: Specific Relief & Limitation
questions.question: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, where, before the expiration of the prescribed period, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of any right is made in writing signed by the party liable, the effect is that:

options.label: A
options.text: the period of limitation is permanently extinguished

options.label: B
options.text: the acknowledgment must be made to the creditor personally to be effective

options.label: C
options.text: a fresh period of limitation begins to run from the time when the acknowledgment was so signed

options.label: D
options.text: the suit becomes maintainable even after the original period has already expired

rectification.principle: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a written and signed acknowledgment made BEFORE expiry of the prescribed limitation period starts a fresh period of limitation from the time of signing (even if not addressed to the creditor).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.18 Limitation Act (acknowledgment before expiry) with s.25(3) Contract Act (written promise to pay a time-barred debt).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.18 = before expiry + signed writing -> fresh limitation runs from signing date.

questions.subject: Specific Relief & Limitation
questions.question: Under Section 17 of the Limitation Act, 1963, where a suit is based upon the fraud of the defendant or the right of action is concealed by fraud, the period of limitation does not begin to run until:

options.label: A
options.text: the date of the fraudulent act itself

options.label: B
options.text: the defendant admits the fraud in writing

options.label: C
options.text: three years from the date of the contract

options.label: D
options.text: the plaintiff has discovered the fraud, or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it

rectification.principle: Section 17 of the Limitation Act, 1963 postpones the commencement of limitation in cases of fraud or mistake until the plaintiff discovers the fraud/mistake or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming limitation always runs strictly from the date the fraudulent transaction occurred.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor s.17 Limitation Act: fraud/mistake -> clock starts upon discovery or reasonable discoverability.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under classical Hindu law, the fundamental distinction between the Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga schools regarding coparcenary is that:

options.label: A
options.text: under Mitakshara a son acquires an interest in coparcenary property by birth, whereas under Dayabhaga he acquires it only on the death of the father

options.label: B
options.text: under Dayabhaga a son acquires an interest by birth, whereas under Mitakshara he acquires it only on the father's death

options.label: C
options.text: both schools confer an interest by birth on the son

options.label: D
options.text: neither school recognises any concept of coparcenary at all

rectification.principle: Under the Mitakshara school, a coparcener acquires an interest in ancestral coparcenary property by birth (with survivorship before 2005 amendment), whereas under the Dayabhaga school (Bengal/Assam), there is no birthright and succession operates only on the father's death.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Reversing the two classical Hindu law schools under exam time pressure.
rectification.howToRectify: Mnemonic: Mitakshara = birthright; Dayabhaga = death of father (D for Death).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: The karta of a Mitakshara joint Hindu family seeks to alienate joint family immovable property. Such an alienation by the karta binds the other coparceners only if it is made:

options.label: A
options.text: entirely at the karta's free discretion without any restriction

options.label: B
options.text: for legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate, or with the consent of the coparceners

options.label: C
options.text: only with the prior written sanction of the civil court in every case

options.label: D
options.text: only after a registered partition deed has been executed

rectification.principle: As settled in Hunoomanpersaud Panday v. Mussumat Babooee (1856), a Karta's alienation of joint family property binds all coparceners only if justified by (1) legal necessity (apatkale), (2) benefit of the estate (kutumbarthe), (3) indispensable religious duties, or with the consent of all coparceners.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the Karta's restricted authority with a guardian's statutory need for court permission under s.8 Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember the Karta trio: legal necessity + benefit of estate + coparceners' consent.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, when a Hindu male dies intestate, his property devolves first upon the heirs specified in:

options.label: A
options.text: Class I of the Schedule

options.label: B
options.text: Class II of the Schedule

options.label: C
options.text: the agnates only

options.label: D
options.text: the cognates only

rectification.principle: Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 prescribes a strict hierarchy for intestate succession of a Hindu male: firstly upon Class I heirs of the Schedule, who take simultaneously to the exclusion of all others.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.8 (male Hindu succession: Class I -> Class II -> Agnates -> Cognates) with s.15 (female Hindu succession).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize Section 8 sequence: Class I -> Class II -> Agnates -> Cognates.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if there is no Class I heir, the property of a Hindu male dying intestate devolves upon:

options.label: A
options.text: the State by escheat immediately

options.label: B
options.text: the cognates in preference to agnates

options.label: C
options.text: the Class I heirs of the deceased's father

options.label: D
options.text: the heirs specified in Class II of the Schedule

rectification.principle: Under Section 8(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if there is no Class I heir, the property devolves upon the relatives specified in Class II of the Schedule (in entry-by-entry order under s.11).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Jumping straight to escheat (which happens only under s.29 when no heir of any class exists) or reversing agnates and cognates.
rectification.howToRectify: Check the four tiers of s.8: (1) Class I, (2) Class II, (3) Agnates, (4) Cognates -> only then s.29 Escheat.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a decree for restitution of conjugal rights may be sought when:

options.label: A
options.text: either spouse has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other

options.label: B
options.text: the marriage has irretrievably broken down

options.label: C
options.text: one spouse has committed a matrimonial offence such as cruelty

options.label: D
options.text: the parties have lived separately for two years

rectification.principle: Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (upheld in Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha, 1984) entitles the aggrieved spouse to seek restitution of conjugal rights when the other has withdrawn from their society without reasonable excuse.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing restitution (s.9, preserving cohabitation) with grounds for divorce (s.13, like cruelty or two years' desertion).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.9 HMA = 'withdrawn from society without reasonable excuse'.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the effect of a decree of judicial separation under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?

options.label: A
options.text: it dissolves the marriage with immediate effect

options.label: B
options.text: it automatically converts into a decree of divorce after six months

options.label: C
options.text: it bars the parties from seeking divorce thereafter

options.label: D
options.text: it does not dissolve the marriage but the petitioner is no longer bound to cohabit with the respondent

rectification.principle: Under Section 10(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a decree of judicial separation keeps the marriage tie intact while relieving the petitioner of the duty to cohabit; non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more becomes a ground for divorce under s.13(1A)(i).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming judicial separation automatically dissolves the marriage after a waiting period without filing a divorce petition under s.13(1A).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Judicial separation = legal pause on cohabitation (not divorce); subsequent divorce requires a separate petition after 1 year.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Among the recognised primary sources of Muslim law, which of the following is the correct descending order of authority?

options.label: A
options.text: Qiyas, Ijma, Sunna, the Quran

options.label: B
options.text: Ijma, the Quran, Qiyas, Sunna

options.label: C
options.text: Sunna, Qiyas, the Quran, Ijma

options.label: D
options.text: the Quran, Sunna (Hadith), Ijma, Qiyas

rectification.principle: The four primary sources of Muslim law stand in strict hierarchical descending authority: (1) The Quran (divine revelation), (2) Sunna/Ahadith (traditions of the Prophet), (3) Ijma (consensus of jurists), and (4) Qiyas (analogical deduction).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Scrambling the positions of Ijma and Qiyas or reversing the order.
rectification.howToRectify: Mnemonic: Revealed sources first (Quran -> Sunna), then human juristic reasoning (Ijma -> Qiyas).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: The two major sects of Muslims are the Sunnis and the Shias. The predominant school of law followed by Sunni Muslims in the Indian subcontinent is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Maliki school

options.label: B
options.text: Shafii school

options.label: C
options.text: Hanafi school

options.label: D
options.text: Ithna Ashari school

rectification.principle: The Hanafi school, founded by Imam Abu Hanifa, is the predominant Sunni school in the Indian subcontinent (courts presume an Indian Sunni Muslim is governed by Hanafi law unless proved otherwise).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the predominant Sunni school in India (Hanafi) with Ithna Ashari (the predominant Shia school).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair the defaults in India: Sunni = Hanafi; Shia = Ithna Ashari.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under Muslim law, a valid hiba (gift) requires three essentials. Which of the following is the correct set?

options.label: A
options.text: a written deed, attestation by two witnesses and registration

options.label: B
options.text: consideration, a written contract and court approval

options.label: C
options.text: declaration by the donor, acceptance by the donee and delivery of possession

options.label: D
options.text: presence of a qazi, payment of mahr and consent of heirs

rectification.principle: Under Muslim law (saved from s.123 TPA by s.129 TPA; Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid), a valid hiba requires three essentials: (1) Ijab (declaration by donor), (2) Qabul (acceptance by donee), and (3) Qabza (delivery of possession)—it may be oral without registration.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying Section 123 Transfer of Property Act (registered written instrument attested by two witnesses) to a Muslim hiba.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.129 TPA exempts Muslim gifts: Hiba needs Declaration + Acceptance + Delivery of Possession.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under Muslim law, after a gift (hiba) has been completed by delivery of possession, the donor may still revoke it in certain cases. However, revocation is NOT permitted where:

options.label: A
options.text: the gift is to a stranger and possession has been given

options.label: B
options.text: the donor has merely changed his mind

options.label: C
options.text: the subject of the gift is movable property

options.label: D
options.text: the donee is a person within prohibited degrees of relationship to the donor (or the spouse)

rectification.principle: Under Hanafi Muslim law, even after delivery of possession, a gift to a stranger may be revoked through court decree/consent, whereas a gift to a spouse or a blood relative within prohibited degrees becomes strictly irrevocable upon completion.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming all gifts once delivered are irrevocable like under TPA, or forgetting the prohibited-degrees/spouse exception.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Hiba to spouse or prohibited blood relative = irrevocable once possession is delivered.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: In Muslim law, a wakf is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: an absolute transfer of ownership of property to another living person

options.label: B
options.text: a temporary lease of property for charitable use for a fixed term

options.label: C
options.text: the permanent dedication of property for a purpose recognised as religious, pious or charitable, the corpus being tied up

options.label: D
options.text: a testamentary disposition operating only after death of the dedicator

rectification.principle: Under the Waqf Act, 1995 and classical Muslim law, a wakf is the permanent dedication by a person professing Islam of movable or immovable property for any purpose recognised by Muslim law as pious, religious, or charitable—tying up the corpus (vested in God) and applying only the usufruct.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing wakf (permanent dedication in perpetuity) with hiba (transfer to a living person) or wasiyat (will).
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor wakf's three traits: permanent (never temporary), corpus tied up in God, pious/religious/charitable object.

questions.subject: Property Law (TPA)
questions.question: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the case of tangible immovable property of a value of one hundred rupees and upwards, a sale can be made only by:

options.label: A
options.text: delivery of possession alone

options.label: B
options.text: an oral agreement followed by part payment

options.label: C
options.text: a registered instrument

options.label: D
options.text: a mere written agreement that need not be registered

rectification.principle: Section 54 TPA mandates that transfer of tangible immovable property of the value of Rs. 100 and upwards (and all intangible immovable property regardless of value) can be made only by a registered instrument.
