rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the rule for tangible immovable property below Rs. 100 (where delivery of possession suffices) with Rs. 100 and upwards.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize s.54 TPA: >= Rs. 100 or intangible = registered instrument mandatory; < Rs. 100 tangible = registered instrument OR delivery of possession.

questions.subject: Property Law (TPA)
questions.question: Under Section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, which of the following is a duty of the seller of immovable property?

options.label: A
options.text: to disclose to the buyer any material defect in the property of which the seller is and the buyer is not aware

options.label: B
options.text: to bear the loss to the property after the date of sale

options.label: C
options.text: to pay the public charges accruing after the date of sale

options.label: D
options.text: to obtain insurance on the property in the buyer's name

rectification.principle: Section 55(1)(a) TPA obligates the seller to disclose to the buyer any material defect in the property or title of which the seller is, and the buyer is not, aware and could not discover with ordinary care (non-disclosure is fraudulent under s.55 last para).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up pre-sale seller duties (s.55(1)) with post-sale buyer risks/charges (s.55(5), where loss and public charges pass to the buyer after ownership passes).
rectification.howToRectify: Separate s.55(1) (seller's duty before sale: disclose latent defects, pay pre-sale charges) from s.55(5) (buyer bears post-sale loss and charges).

questions.subject: Property Law (TPA)
questions.question: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a contract for the sale of immovable property:

options.label: A
options.text: does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property

options.label: B
options.text: operates as an actual transfer of ownership

options.label: C
options.text: by itself creates an interest in or charge on such property

options.label: D
options.text: must always be registered to be enforceable as a contract

rectification.principle: The final paragraph of Section 54 TPA explicitly declares that a contract for sale of immovable property (agreement to sell) 'does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property' (Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing an executed sale deed with an executory agreement to sell (or importing English equitable ownership concepts).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Agreement to sell != sale; it creates only a personal right to specific performance, no interest/charge on property.

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company that has only one person as a member is classified as:

options.label: A
options.text: a public company

options.label: B
options.text: a One Person Company (OPC)

options.label: C
options.text: a company limited by guarantee

options.label: D
options.text: an unlimited company

rectification.principle: Section 2(62) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a 'One Person Company' (OPC) as a company which has only one person as a member (treated as a private company with a named nominee).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing membership-count classification (OPC/Private/Public) with liability classification (guarantee/unlimited).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize s.2(62) Companies Act: 1 member = One Person Company (OPC).

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the clause in the Memorandum of Association that states the objects for which the company is proposed to be incorporated is the:

options.label: A
options.text: object clause

options.label: B
options.text: liability clause

options.label: C
options.text: capital clause

options.label: D
options.text: subscription clause

rectification.principle: Section 4(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the Memorandum of Association to contain the Object Clause, stating the objects for which the company is proposed to be incorporated and matters considered necessary in furtherance thereof.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Basic confusion among the 6 statutory clauses of the MoA under s.4(1).
rectification.howToRectify: Recall all MoA clauses in s.4(1): Name, Registered Office (State), Objects, Liability, Capital, Association/Subscription.

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: The doctrine of ultra vires, as established in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. v. Riche, provides that an act of a company which is beyond the objects stated in its Memorandum is:

options.label: A
options.text: voidable at the option of the company alone

options.label: B
options.text: valid if subsequently ratified by an ordinary resolution

options.label: C
options.text: binding on the company under the doctrine of indoor management

options.label: D
options.text: void and incapable of ratification even by the unanimous consent of all shareholders

rectification.principle: In Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. v. Riche (1875), the House of Lords held that a transaction ultra vires the company's Objects Clause in the Memorandum is wholly void ab initio and cannot be ratified even by the unanimous consent of all shareholders.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing acts ultra vires the Directors (which shareholders CAN ratify) with acts ultra vires the Company's MoA (which CANNOT be ratified).
rectification.howToRectify: Distinguish: Ultra vires the Directors = ratifiable; Ultra vires the Company (MoA) = void ab initio, never ratifiable.

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct minimum number of members for a private company and a public company respectively under the Companies Act, 2013?

options.label: A
options.text: one and seven

options.label: B
options.text: two and seven

options.label: C
options.text: two and three

options.label: D
options.text: seven and two

rectification.principle: Section 3(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a minimum of 7 members for a public company, 2 members for a private company, and 1 member for a One Person Company.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing minimum members (Private: 2, Public: 7) with minimum directors (Private: 2, Public: 3) or OPC (1).
rectification.howToRectify: Keep members vs directors separate: Members = OPC 1 / Private 2 / Public 7; Directors = OPC 1 / Private 2 / Public 3.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists in an original literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work. The requirement of "originality" essentially demands that:

options.label: A
options.text: the work must be entirely novel and never thought of before by anyone

options.label: B
options.text: the work must originate from the author and not be copied from another work

options.label: C
options.text: the work must have been registered with the Copyright Office before any protection arises

options.label: D
options.text: the work must have artistic or literary merit of a high quality

rectification.principle: Under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (University of London Press v. University Tutorial Press; Eastern Book Co. v. D.B. Modak), 'originality' means the expression must originate from the author through independent skill and judgment and not be copied—unlike patents, novelty or literary merit is not required.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Importing Patent Act novelty requirements or assuming copyright registration is mandatory for subsistence.
rectification.howToRectify: Contrast: Patent = absolute novelty; Copyright = originality of expression (not copied), subsists automatically on creation.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, in the case of a literary work made by an author in the course of his employment under a contract of service, the first owner of the copyright is, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary:

options.label: A
options.text: the author who actually created the work

options.label: B
options.text: the Registrar of Copyrights

options.label: C
options.text: the employer

options.label: D
options.text: the Central Government

rectification.principle: While Section 17 of the Copyright Act makes the author the default first owner, proviso (c) to s.17 vests first ownership in the employer when a work is made in the course of employment under a 'contract of service', absent an agreement to the contrary.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying the general rule ('author is first owner') without checking the employment exception in s.17(c).
rectification.howToRectify: Distinguish: Contract FOR service (independent freelancer) -> author owns; Contract OF service (employee) -> employer owns.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under Section 19 of the Copyright Act, 1957, an assignment of copyright is valid only if it is:

options.label: A
options.text: made orally before two witnesses

options.label: B
options.text: in writing and signed by the assignor or his duly authorised agent

options.label: C
options.text: registered with the Trade Marks Registry

options.label: D
options.text: approved by the Copyright Board in every case

rectification.principle: Section 19(1) of the Copyright Act, 1957 mandates that no assignment of copyright shall be valid unless it is in writing signed by the assignor or by his duly authorised agent.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming oral assignments or registry approvals are valid/required for copyright transfers.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.19(1) Copyright Act: assignment = writing + signature of assignor (or agent).

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright in a published literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work (other than a photograph) generally subsists for the lifetime of the author and a further period of:

options.label: A
options.text: fifty years after the year of the author's death

options.label: B
options.text: sixty years after the year of the author's death

options.label: C
options.text: seventy years after the year of the author's death

options.label: D
options.text: twenty years after the year of the author's death

rectification.principle: Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended in 1992), copyright in published literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works subsists for the author's lifetime plus 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Using the Berne Convention minimum (50 years) or US/EU term (70 years) instead of India's statutory 60-year term.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize IP terms in India: Copyright = Life + 60 years; Patent = 20 years; Design = 10 + 5 years.

questions.subject: Consumer Protection Law
questions.question: Under Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a person is NOT a "consumer" where the goods are bought or services availed:

options.label: A
options.text: for a consideration that has been partly paid and partly promised

options.label: B
options.text: for use by a person other than the buyer with the buyer's approval

options.label: C
options.text: by means of an online transaction through an e-commerce platform

options.label: D
options.text: exclusively for the purpose of resale or for any commercial purpose

rectification.principle: Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 includes online/offline transactions, deferred/part consideration, and approved beneficiaries, but expressly excludes anyone obtaining goods for resale or any commercial purpose (except self-employment for livelihood).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Overlooking that online e-commerce purchases and deferred payments are expressly covered under the 2019 definition.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor the core exclusion in s.2(7) CPA: bought for resale or commercial purpose (unless self-employment for livelihood).

questions.subject: Consumer Protection Law
questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds two crore rupees but does not exceed ten crore rupees is to be filed before the:

options.label: A
options.text: District Commission

options.label: B
options.text: State Commission

options.label: C
options.text: National Commission

options.label: D
options.text: civil court of competent jurisdiction

rectification.principle: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (s.34, s.47, s.58), the pecuniary limits based on value of consideration paid are: District Commission up to Rs. 1 crore; State Commission above Rs. 1 crore up to Rs. 10 crore; National Commission above Rs. 10 crore. (Even under the 2021 Rules revision—District up to 50L, State 50L–2Cr, National >2Cr—the question follows the statutory text of CPA 2019 ss.34/47/58: State Commission = Rs. 1–10 crore.)
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing the old 1986 Act slabs (20L / 1Cr) or mixing up State (1–10 Cr in statutory text) and National (>10 Cr in statutory text).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember CPA 2019 statutory slabs (ss.34, 47, 58): District <= 1 Cr; State 1 Cr–10 Cr; National > 10 Cr.

questions.subject: Cyber & IT Law
questions.question: Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, a "digital signature" as defined in Section 2(1)(p) is the authentication of an electronic record by a subscriber by means of:

options.label: A
options.text: a scanned image of the subscriber's handwritten signature

options.label: B
options.text: a one-time password sent to the subscriber's mobile phone

options.label: C
options.text: an electronic method or procedure in accordance with Section 3 (using an asymmetric crypto system and hash function)

options.label: D
options.text: a notarised paper attestation uploaded to a portal

rectification.principle: Section 2(1)(p) read with Section 3 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 defines a 'digital signature' strictly as authentication of an electronic record by a subscriber using an asymmetric crypto system and hash function.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing a statutory cryptographic 'digital signature' with an everyday scanned signature image or OTP.
rectification.howToRectify: Link s.2(1)(p) + s.3 IT Act to two technical terms: asymmetric crypto system + hash function.

questions.subject: Motor Vehicles & Tort Law
questions.question: Under Section 4 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the minimum age at which a person may drive a motorcycle of engine capacity not exceeding 50 cc (without gear) in a public place is:

options.label: A
options.text: sixteen years

options.label: B
options.text: eighteen years

options.label: C
options.text: twenty-one years

options.label: D
options.text: twenty years

rectification.principle: While Section 4(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 sets 18 years as the general minimum driving age, its proviso permits a person who has attained 16 years to drive a motorcycle with engine capacity not exceeding 50 cc without gear.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying the general 18-year driving age without reading the s.4(1) proviso for gearless <=50 cc two-wheelers.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize MV Act s.4 age tiers: 16 (<=50cc gearless), 18 (general motor vehicle), 20 (transport vehicle).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an arbitration agreement that forms part of a larger contract is treated as a distinct agreement, so that even if the main contract is held to be null and void, the arbitration clause survives. This rule is best described as the doctrine of:

options.label: A
options.text: Merger of the arbitration clause into the contract

options.label: B
options.text: Separability (severability) of the arbitration agreement

options.label: C
options.text: Frustration of the arbitration agreement

options.label: D
options.text: Novation of the arbitration agreement

rectification.principle: Section 16(1)(a)–(b) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 codifies the doctrine of separability: an arbitration clause forms an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract, so invalidity of the main contract does not ipso jure invalidate the arbitration clause (Reva Electric Car Co. v. Green Mobil).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking invalidity or termination of the underlying commercial contract automatically kills the arbitration clause.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.16(1) Arbitration Act: Kompetenz-Kompetenz + Separability (arbitration clause stands apart).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following is an essential requirement of a valid arbitration agreement under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?

options.label: A
options.text: It must compulsorily name the sole arbitrator in the agreement itself

options.label: B
options.text: It must be registered before a civil court to be enforceable

options.label: C
options.text: It must be signed before a notary and stamped as a conveyance

options.label: D
options.text: It must be in writing and record the parties' intention to submit present or future disputes to arbitration

rectification.principle: Under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Jagdish Chander v. Ramesh Chander), an arbitration agreement must be in writing and express the parties' binding intention to submit present or future disputes to arbitration; it need not name an arbitrator or be registered/notarised.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming formal registration or naming an arbitrator in advance is legally required.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.7 essentials: In writing (even by letters/electronic means/pleadings) + clear consensus ad idem to arbitrate.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Where an action is brought before a judicial authority in a matter that is the subject of an arbitration agreement, and a party so applies not later than submitting its first statement on the substance of the dispute, the judicial authority shall refer the parties to arbitration. This mandatory reference and stay of the suit is provided in:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: B
options.text: Section 5 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: C
options.text: Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: D
options.text: Section 14 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rectification.principle: Section 8(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 obliges a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration if an application is made not later than submitting the first statement on the substance of the dispute (unless prima facie no valid arbitration agreement exists).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.8 (court referral of pending suit) with s.11 (High Court/SC appointment of arbitrator) or s.5 (extent of judicial intervention).
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize Part I early sections: s.5 minimal intervention, s.7 agreement, s.8 refer to arbitration, s.9 court interim relief, s.11 appoint arbitrator.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A party apprehends that the opposite party may dissipate the subject matter of the dispute even before the arbitral tribunal is constituted. The party may apply to a court for interim measures of protection under which provision?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 17 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: B
options.text: Section 27 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: C
options.text: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

options.label: D
options.text: Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996

rectification.principle: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 empowers a court to grant interim measures of protection before, during, or after arbitral proceedings prior to enforcement (Sundaram Finance v. NEPC India, 1999)—making it the sole interim remedy before the tribunal is constituted.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.9 (interim relief by Court) with s.17 (interim relief by Arbitral Tribunal once constituted).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair s.9 (Court interim measures—available even before tribunal exists) vs s.17 (Tribunal interim measures—only during proceedings).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (as amended in 2015), the power of the arbitral tribunal itself to order interim measures of protection during the proceedings, with the same enforceability as an order of court, is contained in:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 9

options.label: B
options.text: Section 16

options.label: C
options.text: Section 17

options.label: D
options.text: Section 19

rectification.principle: Amended Section 17 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (post-2015 Amendment) gives the arbitral tribunal full power to grant interim measures during proceedings and deems its order enforceable as an order of the Court under CPC.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Mixing up s.9 (Court's interim power) with s.17 (Tribunal's interim power).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: s.9 = Court; s.17 = Arbitral Tribunal (with court-like enforceability post-2015).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Section 18 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 enshrines a fundamental safeguard rooted in natural justice. It requires that:

options.label: A
options.text: The arbitrator must always be a retired judge

options.label: B
options.text: The parties shall be treated with equality and each party shall be given a full opportunity to present its case

options.label: C
options.text: The award must be delivered within thirty days

options.label: D
options.text: The proceedings must be held only in the language of the contract

rectification.principle: Section 18 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 ('Equal treatment of parties') mandates that parties be treated with equality and each party be given a full opportunity to present its case.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.18 (natural justice) with s.22 (language) or s.29A (12-month timeline).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.18 Arbitration Act: 'Equality + Full opportunity to present case'.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The fast-track procedure, under which parties may agree to have their dispute resolved within six months on the basis of written pleadings and documents, ordinarily without an oral hearing, was inserted by the 2015 Amendment as:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 29A

options.label: B
options.text: Section 31A

options.label: C
options.text: Section 33

options.label: D
options.text: Section 29B

rectification.principle: Section 29B of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (inserted in 2015) provides the optional fast-track procedure: award within 6 months based on written pleadings/documents without oral hearing unless requested/needed.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.29A (standard 12-month time limit for arbitral award) with s.29B (6-month fast-track procedure).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair ss.29A & 29B: 29A = 12-month normal timeline; 29B = 6-month fast-track documents-only procedure.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics
questions.question: Under Section 24 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which of the following is a qualification for a person to be admitted as an advocate on a State roll?

options.label: A
options.text: He must have completed sixty years of age

options.label: B
options.text: He must be a citizen of India and, subject to the proviso, have completed the age of twenty-one years and obtained a degree in law from a recognised University

options.label: C
options.text: He must already be enrolled with the Bar Council of India

options.label: D
options.text: He must have practised as a clerk for at least five years

rectification.principle: Section 24(1) of the Advocates Act, 1961 prescribes the core qualifications for enrolment on a State roll: citizen of India, completed 21 years of age, and obtained a recognised degree in law (plus fulfilling any State Bar Council conditions).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Misunderstanding enrolment jurisdiction (advocates enrol on a State roll first, not directly with BCI).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember s.24(1) Advocates Act triad: Citizen of India + 21 years + Recognised LL.B. degree.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics
questions.question: Section 24A of the Advocates Act, 1961 lays down disqualifications for enrolment. A person is disqualified from being enrolled as an advocate if he:

options.label: A
options.text: Has been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude (subject to the period prescribed)

options.label: B
options.text: Is below thirty years of age

options.label: C
options.text: Holds a part-time teaching post in law

options.label: D
options.text: Has not enrolled within one year of obtaining the law degree

rectification.principle: Section 24A of the Advocates Act, 1961 disqualifies a person from enrolment if convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude, or under the Untouchability (Offences) Act, or dismissed/removed from government employment on charges involving moral turpitude (until 2 years after release/dismissal).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing permissible activities (like part-time law teaching) with statutory disqualifications under s.24A.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor s.24A Advocates Act: conviction/dismissal for moral turpitude = bar to enrolment (subject to the 2-year cooling period).

questions.subject: Professional Ethics
questions.question: Under the Advocates Act, 1961, the power to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates, and to lay down the procedure to be followed by its disciplinary committee and that of each State Bar Council, is a function of:

options.label: A
options.text: The State Bar Council under Section 6

options.label: B
options.text: The Supreme Court under Section 38

options.label: C
options.text: The Central Government under Section 49A

options.label: D
options.text: The Bar Council of India under Section 7

rectification.principle: Section 7(1)(b) and (c) of the Advocates Act, 1961 entrusts the Bar Council of India with laying down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates and the procedure for its disciplinary committee and those of State Bar Councils.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing Section 6 (functions of State Bar Council: admission & maintenance of rolls) with Section 7 (functions of Bar Council of India).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair ss.6–7 Advocates Act: s.6 = State Bar Council (enrolment); s.7 = Bar Council of India (national standards & disciplinary procedure).

questions.subject: Professional Ethics
questions.statuteRef: BCI Rules (Part VI, Ch. II, Rules 25–30)
questions.question: An advocate receives a sum of money from his client to be applied towards court fees and incidental expenses. Under the Bar Council of India Rules on an advocate's duty to the client, the advocate is bound to:

options.label: A
options.text: Keep accounts of the client's money entrusted to him and render an account, refunding any unspent balance

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the money as his professional fee and need not account for it

options.label: C
options.text: Adjust the money against future briefs without informing the client

options.label: D
options.text: Retain the entire sum as a lien irrespective of the work done

rectification.principle: Under Rules 25–30 (Chapter II, Part VI) of the Bar Council of India Rules, an advocate stands in a fiduciary position: money entrusted by a client for expenses/court fees must be accounted for separately, applied only as instructed, and any unspent balance must be refunded (never silently converted into fees).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing an advocate's right to agreed fees (s.28/BCI Rules) with money held in trust for client expenses.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: client's expense money is held in trust—must keep accounts and refund unspent balance.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics
questions.question: Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, wilful disobedience of a judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court, or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court, amounts to:

options.label: A
options.text: Criminal contempt under Section 2(c)

options.label: B
options.text: A mere execution default attracting no contempt

options.label: C
options.text: Civil contempt under Section 2(b)

options.label: D
options.text: Constructive contempt outside the Act

rectification.principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines 'civil contempt' as wilful disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court (Ashok Paper Kamgar Union v. Dharam Godha).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.2(b) civil contempt (wilful disobedience of court order/undertaking) with s.2(c) criminal contempt (scandalising the court or interfering with administration of justice).
rectification.howToRectify: Pair s.2(b) & s.2(c): s.2(b) = Civil contempt (disobeying order/undertaking); s.2(c) = Criminal contempt (scandalising/obstructing justice).
